summary:
Düzce stands under the national framework of Turkey. The source inventory for this province records no Düzce-specific incident, enforcement practice or local instrument, so the assessment rests on the national regime a visitor to Düzce is subject to.

Consensual same-sex activity has been legal in Turkey since the 1858 Ottoman penal code, and legal gender change has been available since 1988. Turkish marriage law gives same-sex relationships no legal recognition and provides no civil unions, domestic partnerships or joint adoption. No comprehensive law bans discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and LGBTQ people are barred from open military service.

In early 2026 Turkish media reported that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex'; that provision was not included in that year's judicial reform package. Pride events and LGBTQ gatherings were repeatedly disallowed in 2024 and 2025, with police detaining participants, per Amnesty International.
tangentialFactors:
The national framework recorded above is the same one under which roughly 20 trans women were stopped by police in Istanbul's Beyoğlu district in August 2025, held at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released after background checks recorded without any offence being cited. The checks were described by legal experts quoted by bianet as breaching Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 records 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions. Turkish Minute's coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. These are national figures and are not specific to Düzce.
localsOnly:
Residents of Düzce live under the same national framework: no comprehensive discrimination protection on sexual orientation or gender identity, no recognition of same-sex relationships, and no route to open military service for LGBTQ people. Legal gender change has been available nationally since 1988.

Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans residents must obtain and pay for it privately. Detainees are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare, with no policy or staff training to identify LGBTI+ needs.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the draft legislative package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, which would effectively criminalise LGBT people under provisions protecting 'the family' and 'public morals', has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

The source inventory contains no Düzce-specific enforcement data, local ordinance, or incident record; the province-level assessment is therefore an application of the national framework rather than a finding about Düzce itself.
